Analysis & Interpretation of Data

Analyzing and interpreting research data — editing, coding, descriptive and inferential statistics, tables and discussion.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Prepare data for analysis
  • Calculate descriptive statistics
  • Choose appropriate inferential tests
  • Present results and interpret findings

In simple words

Analysis turns numbers or words into findings. Preparation first: check for errors, missing answers and outliers. Then describe, compare and interpret.

Steps in data analysis

  1. Editing — check for completeness and errors
  2. Classification and coding — group responses and assign numbers
  3. Tabulation — make master tables
  4. Descriptive statistics — summarise the sample
  5. Inferential statistics — test differences and relationships
  6. Interpretation — what do the findings mean

Descriptive statistics

Measure What it gives
Frequency How often things happen
Percentage Share of the total
Mean Average
Median Middle value
Mode Most frequent value
Range Highest minus lowest
Standard deviation Spread of values around the mean

Inferential statistics — choosing a test

Purpose Test
Compare two group means Independent samples t-test
Compare paired means Paired t-test
Compare two proportions (nominal) Chi-square test
Compare three or more groups ANOVA
Relationship between two numbers Pearson r
Ranked or ordinal data Mann-Whitney, Spearman
Predict from two or more factors Regression

Level of significance: most nursing studies use p less than 0.05. A p value is the probability that a result happened by chance. If p is less than 0.05, the result is called statistically significant.

🔴 Significance is not importance

A statistically significant result may be too small to matter clinically, while a meaningful result may fail to reach significance in a small sample. Always discuss the actual size of the change, not only the p value.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Analysis starts with editing, coding and tabulation.
  2. Mean is the average; median is the middle value; mode is the most frequent.
  3. Standard deviation shows how spread out the values are.
  4. Chi-square compares proportions; t-test compares means.
  5. A p value under 0.05 is usually taken as statistically significant.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. ANOVA compares three or more groups.
  2. Pearson r shows correlation between two numeric variables.
  3. Tables, charts and graphs make results readable.
  4. Qualitative data are analysed by themes.
  5. Limitations and recommendations complete the discussion.

📌 Memory trick

Describe then compare: D-M-S — Describe (mean, SD), Means (t-test), Shares (chi-square).

60-second revision

  • Prepare data: edit, code, tabulate.
  • Describe: frequency, percentage, mean, median, mode, SD.
  • Test: t-test, chi-square, ANOVA, correlation, regression.
  • p under 0.05 is significant.
  • Present in tables and graphs; interpret with limits.

Test yourself

The middle value of an ordered data set is the:

Answer: B. The median is the middle value when data are ordered.

A study compares mean pain scores of two independent groups. The test is:

Answer: B. The independent samples t-test compares means of two independent groups.

A result with a p value of 0.03 is:

Answer: B. Since 0.03 is less than 0.05, the result is statistically significant.

Which statistic measures the spread of values?

Answer: B. Standard deviation measures how spread the values are around the mean.

Chi-square is used to compare:

Answer: B. The chi-square test compares proportions or frequencies across categories.
